title: Factfulness: Ten Reasons We're Wrong About the World – and Why Things Are Better Than You Think
author: Hans Rosling, with Ola Rosling and Anna Rosling Rönnlund
target_audience: General readers interested in global trends
Professionals in media and public health
Anyone seeking a data-driven, optimistic view of the world
primary_purpose: To challenge common myths and misconceptions about the world using factual data, and to encourage readers to adopt a fact-based, nuanced, and hopeful perspective on global progress and contemporary issues.

structure_format.narrative_style: Engaging, conversational, personal anecdotes interwoven with rigorous data analysis
structure_format.organization: Divided into ten chapters, each addressing a specific instinct or cognitive bias that leads to misunderstandings about the world

key_concepts_lessons: The world is systematically better than we often think—poverty, health, and education have improved globally.
Ten main instincts (e.g., gap, negativity, straight line, fear, size, generalization, destiny, single perspective, blame, urgency) distort our view of reality.
Media and personal biases amplify dramatic, negative stories.
Making data-based decisions leads to better understanding and improved outcomes.
Factfulness is a skill that anyone can cultivate to counteract innate biases.
Progress is gradual and complex, not dependent on simple narratives.
notable_features: Fact-based quizzes to reveal knowledge gaps
Personal and professional stories from global health and education projects
Secular, nonpartisan, and focused on universal human progress
cultural_historical_context: Published in an era of widespread misinformation, polarization, and pessimism about global trends, the book responded to a cultural need for data-driven optimism and intellectual humility in public discourse. Hans Rosling leveraged his decades of work in global health and development, along with the accessible Gapminder Foundation tools, to counteract misconceptions.
reception_impact: International bestseller translated into dozens of languages
Endorsed by Bill Gates, Barack Obama, and many educators
Widely used in schools and universities to teach data literacy
Praised for clarity, accessibility, and positive outlook
Sparked discussions about media responsibility and public understanding of data
comparable_titles: Enlightenment Now: The Case for Reason, Science, Humanism, and Progress by Steven Pinker
The Rational Optimist by Matt Ridley
The Numbers Don’t Lie by Vaclav Smil
Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction by Philip E. Tetlock and Dan Gardner
